results.message: How does this chatbot work under the hood?
results.text:
Under the hood, I built it as a **two-step pipeline**:

- First, a structured JSON classifier routes the question to the right path.
- Then a grounded answer prompt streams the response back.

I also layered in a few defenses against prompt injection:

- preflight heuristics
- nonce-tagged delimiters
- a streaming canary scanner
- least-context data selection

On the quality side, I versioned the prompts and tuned them with an eval suite of deterministic graders. In v2, that moved the suite from **52% to 98%**.

The core is test-driven too — I covered the guards, prompt contract, and API route with unit tests using mocked models.

results.message: How did you design the system prompt for JustinGPT?
results.text:
I designed JustinGPT around a **two-step pipeline** instead of asking one big prompt to do everything.

- First, a **structured-JSON classifier** routes each question to the right path.

- I also built in layered **prompt-injection defenses**: preflight heuristics, nonce-tagged delimiters, a streaming canary scanner, and least-context data selection.
- On top of that, I kept the prompts **versioned** and tuned them with an eval suite of deterministic graders.

That setup mattered because I wanted the chatbot to behave like a real living resume: accurate, resilient, and able to answer follow-up questions without drifting off into nonsense.

results.message: How did you design the system prompt for JustinGPT?
results.text:
I designed JustinGPT around a **grounded, two-step flow** instead of letting one big prompt do everything.

- First, a **structured-JSON classifier** decides what kind of question it is.
- Then a **separate answer prompt** streams the response using only the relevant, allowed info.
- I added **layered prompt-injection defenses**: preflight heuristics, nonce-tagged delimiters, a streaming canary scanner, and least-context data selection.
- I also versioned the prompts and tuned them with an **eval suite of deterministic graders**; that work took the suite from **52% to 98%**.
- The whole core is **test-driven**, so the guardrails, prompt contract, and API route are all covered with unit tests using mocked models.

So the system prompt wasn’t just “be helpful” — it was part of a fairly defensive, tightly scoped pipeline.

results.message: What do you know about defending against prompt injection?
results.text:
I’ve spent a decent amount of time thinking about it while building **JustinGPT**.

My approach is layered:

- **Preflight heuristics** to catch obviously sketchy inputs early
- **Nonce-tagged delimiters** so the model has clearer boundaries around trusted content
- A **streaming canary scanner** to catch leaks while the response is being generated
- **Least-context data selection**, so I only pass in the minimum needed
- **Versioned prompts** with an eval suite, so I can measure whether defenses actually hold up
- **Unit tests** around every guard, prompt contract, and the API route

That setup helped a newer prompt version move my eval suite from **52% to 98%**.

results.message: What do you know about defending against prompt injection?
results.text:
I’ve built prompt-injection defenses into **JustinGPT**. My approach is layered:

- **Preflight heuristics** to catch suspicious inputs early
- **Nonce-tagged delimiters** to separate trusted content from untrusted content
- A **streaming canary scanner** to detect jailbreak-style leakage while the answer is being generated
- **Least-context data selection** so the model only sees what it needs

I also version my prompts and run them through an **eval suite** with deterministic graders, so I can measure whether the defenses are actually holding up. In my setup, v2 took the suite from **52% to 98%**.

results.message: What do you know about defending against prompt injection?
results.text:
I’ve put some thought into prompt injection while building **JustinGPT**.

My defenses are layered:

- **Preflight heuristics** to catch risky input early
- **Nonce-tagged delimiters** to separate trusted content from user text
- A **streaming canary scanner** to watch for unexpected leakage as the response is generated
- **Least-context data selection** so the model only sees what it needs

I also version prompts and run them through an eval suite of deterministic graders. That work really mattered: **v2 improved the suite from 52% to 98%**.

So my general philosophy is: don’t rely on one silver bullet—stack defenses, keep the prompt surface area small, and test the whole thing like code.
